v.q: `String a = "ACC"; String b = new String("ACC");` What do `a == b` and `a.equals(b)` return?
v.w: `==` compares references, and `new String` creates a separate heap object. `equals` compares the characters.
== compares references. equals compares the characters. new always creates a distinct object.

v.q: A method receives `String input` that may be `null`. Which comparison is safe?
v.w: Call `equals` on the known non-null literal, or use `Objects.equals`. The other forms throw or compare references.

v.q: Which comparison avoids a NullPointerException when input might be null?
v.w: Objects.equals handles null on either side. Calling a method on null input throws.

v.q: Why is building a 10,000-line report with `s = s + line` in a loop slow?
o: Each pass creates a new String and copies everything built so far
Strings are stored on disk until the loop completes
The `+` operator locks the string pool on every pass
Java converts each line to bytes before appending it
v.w: That is O(n²) copying plus garbage. A `StringBuilder` appends in place and creates one String at the end.

v.q: Which is the best fix for slow string concatenation in a loop?
v.w: StringBuilder appends into a growing buffer instead of copying the whole string each time.

v.q: Which is NOT a reason why `String` is immutable?
o: It makes string concatenation faster than with a builder
It lets literals be shared safely in the string pool
It allows the hash code to be cached for map keys
It makes strings safe to share between threads
v.w: Immutability actually makes repeated modification more expensive, which is why `StringBuilder` exists.

v.q: Which is a real reason why String is immutable?
o: It lets the hash code be cached
It makes concatenation faster than a builder
It lets strings be modified in place
v.w: A fixed value means the hash can be cached, literals can be pooled and strings are safe to share between threads.

o: `true`: the compiler folds constants into the pooled literal
`false`: concatenation always creates a new object
It does not compile because `+` needs a variable
v.w: Constant expressions are evaluated at compile time. With a non-final variable the concatenation happens at run time and gives a new object.

v.q: Given String b = "b";, which expression is false?
v.w: A concatenation with a variable is computed at run time and creates a new object, so == fails. Constants are folded at compile time.

v.q: `"a.b".split(".")` returns an empty array. What is the cause?
o: The argument is a regex where `.` matches any character
`split` only accepts single characters, not strings
The string has no whitespace to split on
`split` drops every part that has a punctuation mark
v.w: Escape it: `split("\\.")`. `replace` takes literal text, while `replaceAll` and `split` take regular expressions.
split takes a regex, so a literal dot must be escaped. A bare dot matches any character.

v.q: Which design step is required to make this class truly immutable? `class Statement { private final List<Entry> entries; Statement(List<Entry> e) { entries = e; } }`
o: Copy the list in the constructor, e.g. `List.copyOf(e)`
Declare the list field as `volatile` instead of final
Add a synchronized getter for the list field
Store the list in a static field of the class
v.w: `final` only fixes the reference. A caller who keeps the original list can still change it, so make a defensive immutable copy.

v.q: Which getter keeps a class holding a List field immutable?
o: Returns an unmodifiable copy or view of the list
Returns the list as an Object
Returns a reference to a static list
v.w: Handing out the internal list lets callers change it, so return List.copyOf or an unmodifiable view.

v.q: Which type is the right choice for money amounts?
v.w: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly. BigDecimal does decimal arithmetic.
